title: GIGAWATT Player Wiki
text: GIGAWATT Player Wiki A practical guide to building, powering and leasing out an AI datacenter from 2020 to 2028. GIGAWATT is a tycoon game about the whole AI hardware stack: you buy real GPUs, NICs and switches from a catalogue of 690+ parts and 100 vendors, design server trays and racks, power and cool a hall, wire a fabric into a supercomputer, and lease capacity to customers who train and serve models. The campaign runs December 2020 to December 2028 and ends with a scored report covering net worth, reliability and scale. If you are not sure what to do first, read Getting started getting started.md , then follow Your first hour first hour.md step by step. Every other page digs into one system of the game. The hall img/hall.png Your hall: every rack labelled by hardware and customer. The wiki Basics Getting started getting started.md — install, first launch, modes, the HUD, the eight drawers, camera, saves Your first hour first hour.md — a guided walk from an empty hall to your first revenue, following the Learning path Building the plant Power and cooling power and cooling.md — transformers, UPS and generators, PUE, CRAH, RDHx, DLC and chillers, and why heat caps everything Servers and racks servers and racks.md — trays, rack density, the Design Lab, validation and spares Networking and clusters networking and clusters.md — scale up vs scale out, fabrics, oversubscription and the Supercomputer screen Selling capacity Customers and contracts customers and contracts.md — training vs inference offers, fit verdicts, the Easy Path, SLAs, renewals and the ramp window Energy and the spot market energy and spot.md — PPAs, take or pay, spot power and selling idle GPUs Running the business Money and operations money and operations.md — cash, loans, depreciation, staffing, hardware lifecycle and the Operations screen Hardware roadmap hardware roadmap.md — keynotes, pre orders, lead times, allocation and when to buy Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md — fires, chiller trips, supply shocks, defaults and how to prepare Reference Strategy tips strategy tips.md — habits of successful operators FAQ faq.md — fifteen common questions, answered Glossary glossary.md — forty one datacenter terms in one line each Where things live in the game The bottom dock has eight buttons: Overview the 3D hall , Customers , Supply Procure and Warehouse , Facility Build and Energy , Operations , Design Lab , Supercomputer and Codex . The Codex glossary.md inside the game also has a "Datacenter 101" view that tells you, live, whether you need each concept right now — when this wiki and the Codex disagree, trust the Codex, because it can see your hall. Ready? Start with Getting started getting started.md .

title: Getting started
text: Getting started Installing GIGAWATT, picking a mode, and finding your way around the HUD, drawers, camera and saves. The Overview drawer. The "Needs you now" card at the top is img/overview needs.png The Overview drawer. The "Needs you now" card at the top is the one thing worth doing next; everything below it folds away. Install and run Grab the archive for your OS from the game's Releases page, extract it, and run the launcher inside — Node.js is bundled, so there is nothing else to install. OS Run Windows GIGAWATT\GIGAWATT.exe SmartScreen: More info → Run anyway Linux GIGAWATT/gigawatt.sh needs a Vulkan capable GPU and driver macOS Remove the quarantine attribute from the app, then open it Builds are unsigned, so expect a warning from your OS the first time. From source, you need Godot 4.x and Node 18+, and you launch with godot path godot . The title screen and modes You pick one of three modes when starting a campaign, and you can cycle between them any time from the top bar: Learner — "I don't know what a chiller is." Explainers everywhere, the most starting cash, and no bankruptcy risk: Learner runs cannot go bankrupt. Operator — "I know the basics." A guided procurement planner, checklists and a moderate bankroll. The recommended first mode. Tycoon — "Just give me the keys." The least starting cash and no hand holding. The Easy Path on the Customers screen, which orders, installs, deploys and assigns contracts for you, is available in every mode. A short guided tutorial walks a first run from the first customer to the first revenue, then hands over to the Learning path missions see Your first hour first hour.md . If a recent save exists, CONTINUE resumes exactly where you left off, tutorial included. The HUD The top bar is always visible: Date and month progress — the campaign runs Dec 2020 → Dec 2028, one month at a time. CASH, DEBT, NET WORTH, REPUTATION ★ — your four vital signs. Reputation rises when you deliver contracts and falls with SLA misses and incidents. Speed controls — pause, 1×, 2×, 3× auto advance, and the big NEXT MONTH button. Nothing happens until you advance a month; this is a turn based game with a 3D view. Mode, How to play, Sound, Save, MENU — self explanatory; Save writes to the slot you last saved to or loaded from. Toasts appear top right for deliveries, incidents and mission completions, and a keynote overlay pauses the clock when a hardware launch lands see Hardware roadmap hardware roadmap.md . The eight drawers Press the number key or click the dock. Pressing the key of the open drawer again closes it and returns you to the Overview. Key Drawer What's inside 1 Overview Datacenter The 3D hall, cash plaques, a next month preview, Learning path missions, Easy path projects, customers and the event log 2 Customers Market offers with live fit verdicts, contracts, assignment 3 Supply Procure guided planner, parts bin, roadmap and Warehouse assembly, deploy, spares, ledger 4 Facility Build power, cooling, floor space, internet, halls and Energy PPAs, spot market 5 Operations Team, debt, hardware lifecycle, operating policy, vendors, rivals 6 Design Lab Full screen tray bench and rack bench with live validation 7 Supercomputer Full screen cluster builder: racks + fabric = one machine 8 Codex Full screen parts encyclopedia, "Datacenter 101" concepts, accelerator timeline 0 also opens it Camera and the hall The game opens in top view with every rack labelled by hardware and customer. Left drag or WASD pans, right drag orbits, wheel zooms, Q/E rotates, V returns to top view, L toggles rack labels, and T switches to the thermal view that shows heat. Click a rack to inspect it: serial, status, what it is doing, a spot market toggle and a decommission button. A gamepad works too A select, B back, X inspect, Y next month, LB/RB drawers . Keyboard shortcuts Space — next month 1 – 8 — open/close drawers · 0 — open the Codex Q / E — rotate the hall · WASD — pan · V / L / T — top view / labels / thermal view Esc — pause menu · F1 — settings and controls · Ctrl+Q — quit Saves Saves are versioned and stored in your user data folder: three manual slots plus a monthly autosave . Quitting or closing the window always writes the autosave first, so it never overwrites a manual slot. Save from the top bar or the pause menu; load from the title screen or the pause menu. Settings F1 opens settings: master/music/effects volume, a music style picker the soundtrack follows the game — expect something darker when things fail , UI scale, a colour blind safe cluster palette, reduced motion, and graphics quality Low/Balanced/High. Next: Your first hour first hour.md .

title: Your first hour
text: Your first hour A step by step walkthrough from an empty hall to your first revenue, following the Learning path missions in order. The Missions panel on the Overview screen always shows your next three missions with a Go → button that jumps to the right screen. Each completed mission pays a cash reward and teaches one lesson. This page walks the opening ten in order. If you ever feel stuck, the Easy Path customers and contracts.md on the Customers screen can order, install, deploy and assign a contract for you. Every January a chapter card sets the scene for the year ahe img/story chapter.png Every January a chapter card sets the scene for the year ahead. 1 · Place your first order Procure Open Supply → Procure . The guided planner walks you through: pick a platform a GPU generation, pre engineered , say how many accelerators you want, choose how to buy — DIY cheapest, you integrate , an OEM integrated rack, or turnkey priciest, fastest — check your hall can feed and cool it, then order from the bill of materials. The lesson: hardware has lead times and, for GPUs, allocation . Parts arrive months later, so order early. The guided planner img/procure.png Platform → how many → how to buy → hall check → order. 2 · Expand your cooling plant Build Open Facility → Build . Under Buy plant , buy a CRAH air handler sized for your hall's cooling class, wait for it to arrive, then Install 1 from inventory. Every watt of IT power becomes a watt of heat, and cooling capacity — not floor space — caps most AI halls. See Power and cooling power and cooling.md . 3 · Design a server tray Design Lab Open Design Lab → Tray bench . Pick an 8 GPU chassis, hit Auto fill to populate every required socket, then fix anything the live validation flags. The Sizing advisor checks PSU capacity and N+1 redundancy, PCIe lanes versus CPU count, NIC bandwidth per GPU, and memory. Save the tray. Details in Servers and racks servers and racks.md . 4 · Design a rack Design Lab Switch to the Rack bench . Stack your trays plus a leaf top of rack switch into a 42U elevation within the rack's kW limit — four 8 GPU H100 trays at roughly 10 kW each already push 40 kW. Set the cooling interface, clear the validation errors, and save the rack design. 5 · Place a rack on the floor Warehouse Open Supply → Warehouse . Your rack design lists exactly which parts are missing; use order all missing to buy them in one go. When everything is in the warehouse and the hall has power, cooling and a free slot, press DEPLOY 1 or pick the design on the Build screen and click an empty floor slot . 6 · Get a rack online Racks take months to install and commission. Press Space to advance months and watch the Next month preview on the Overview screen — it tells you what is arriving, what starts burn in and what goes online. Commissioning power on, firmware, burn in is what finds dead GPUs before your customers do; you control its length in Operations. Build screen ledger img/build ledger.png Every rack's serial, slot, status and current job, on the Build screen. 7 · Build a cluster Supercomputer Open Supercomputer , select your online rack s , press Auto design for TRAINING or the cheaper inference fabric , check the What can this machine do? table, and BUILD CLUSTER . A cluster is racks plus a network fabric — see Networking and clusters networking and clusters.md . 8 · Land your first contract Customers Open Customers and read the verdict on each offer: CAN SERVE NOW , CAN BUILD IN TIME , or NEED MORE / DIFFERENT HARDWARE . If you're ready, SIGN & START SERVING and assign your cluster. If not, the What you need to buy box lists the exact racks to order — or press EASY PATH and the game does the whole pipeline for you. You can also serve straight from racks without clustering. Inference is memory bandwidth bound; training is compute and network bound — match hardware to workload. 9 · Sign a power contract Energy Open Facility → Energy . Compare plant offers solar, gas, hydro, nuclear, grid and sign a PPA roughly matched to your draw. Take or pay means you pay for committed megawatts whether you use them or not, so don't over commit. More in Energy and the spot market energy and spot.md . 10 · Earn revenue Advance a month with an active contract. Revenue minus power, staff, support, depreciation and interest is your profit — the plaques at the bottom of the Overview screen show revenue, burn and net per month. Utilization is everything: an idle rack still costs money, so put spare capacity on the spot market. After the first hour The Learning path continues: go liquid cooled with a DLC hall and a 120 kW class rack, run a 256 accelerator supercomputer, deploy a 72 GPU NVLink domain, then the long campaign goals thousands of accelerators, halls, net worth . See Strategy tips strategy tips.md .

title: Power and cooling
text: Power and cooling Transformers, UPS and generators, PUE, CRAH, RDHx, direct to chip liquid and chillers — and why heat, not floor space, is what limits your hall. Every watt a GPU draws turns into a watt of heat inside your hall. The Build screen has two gauges that matter more than anything else: IT load vs your power feed and heat rejection vs installed cooling . If racks draw more than the feed, breakers trip or racks throttle. If heat rejection is below IT load, hardware fails roughly three times more often. Both gauges warn you as you approach the limit. Transformer / switchgear — the power feed The transformer steps utility voltage down to what the hall uses and sets the maximum IT load in kW you may draw. It arrives in your warehouse after a lead time and is installed from the Build screen. Plan feed capacity ahead of rack purchases — transformers have lead times measured in months, and a 100 MW campus starts with grid interconnection and transformers ordered years ahead. UPS, batteries and generators Grid power blips. Customers sign SLAs at 95–99.5% availability, and a grid dip without protection restarts every training job. The protection chain, all visible in the Outage protection panel: UPS — batteries or flywheels that ride through dips; needs both inverter capacity and a battery string sized to IT load Generator — takes over for long outages; must be sized to at least your IT load Transfer switch ATS/STS — moves load to the generator automatically N+1 — a second generator that can parallel or an oversized UPS , so any single engine, battery string or chiller can fail with zero customer impact; this is what enterprise and sovereign customers pay for The panel shows your tier none / basic / N / N+1 , the share of outages you ride through, and exactly which gap is holding you back. Enterprise contracts with SLAs at 98%+ expect this chain before you sign. PUE — the number on your bill PUE = total facility power ÷ IT power. A perfect hall would score 1.0; 1.1–1.5 is typical. You pay for the overhead — cooling, conversion losses — on top of IT power every single month, so a lower PUE efficient cooling, liquid instead of air at density directly cuts your power bill. Each hall's PUE shows on its Build panel. The cooling ladder Cooling classes are set per hall when you build it air, RDHx, DLC, immersion , and each class has its own equipment: Class Works up to How CRAH air ~20–25 kW per rack Air handlers push cold air under the floor and pull hot air back Rear door heat exchanger ~40 kW per rack A water coil on the rack's back door cools exhaust before it re enters the room — no server plumbing DLC direct to chip 40 kW and beyond Coolant flows through cold plates on GPUs/CPUs; a CDU coolant distribution unit isolates and pumps the loop Immersion highest densities Servers submerged in dielectric fluid Air cannot carry away 40+ kW from one rack. GB200 NVL72 racks ~120 kW are liquid only: they need a DLC hall, CDUs, and a floor planned for the loop — the same rack format continues with later generations. Chillers and cooling towers CRAHs and CDUs don't destroy heat, they move it. Past a certain heat load — or in any liquid cooled hall — you need a central plant: a chiller makes cold water, and a cooling tower or dry cooler throws the heat to outside air. Chiller trips are a real incident see Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md ; N+1 chillers with automatic switchover keep the water cold while one unit is repaired. Thermal view img/thermal.png Press T: the thermal view shows where your heat actually is. Rear door heat exchangers img/campus rdhx.png An RDHx hall — water coils on the rack doors stretch air cooling to denser racks. Reading the screen The gauges turn red when you exceed feed or cooling; the ≥80% zone is your cue to expand Hall checks lists validation issues for the selected hall Floor space is bought in blocks with a commissioning delay — but space is rarely your real limit The Codex → Datacenter 101 view gives a live "do I need this right now?" verdict for every concept on this page, with a Show me where jump Related: Servers and racks servers and racks.md for rack density, Energy and the spot market energy and spot.md for what power costs.

title: Servers and racks
text: Servers and racks Trays, racks, the Design Lab, rack density, validation and spares — how the machines you sell are actually made. There are two ways to get hardware: buy a pre engineered system the Procure guided planner's DIY / OEM / turnkey tiers, or ready made templates from several integrators , or design your own in the Design Lab . Buying a system saves its design automatically, so you can study it, copy it and modify it — a good way to learn. The tray bench A tray is a chassis plus parts. Pick a chassis its cooling class and rack units matter , then click sockets on the board and install parts: accelerators, CPUs, DIMMs, NICs, DPUs, NVMe drives, PSUs. Required slots are marked; Auto fill populates everything with the first compatible part, and load pre built system starts you from a known good design. Live validation refuses to save a broken tray. It tracks power draw, cost, accelerator count, FP8/BF16 PFLOPS, HBM and PCIe lanes. The Sizing & cost advisor is the teaching tool — it checks, as you build: PSUs — capacity must cover the GPU draw with N+1 redundancy: one PSU can fail without taking down an expensive tray. More than N+1 is wasted money. PCIe lanes and CPUs — GPUs set the power and NIC needs, CPUs set lanes and memory channels. One CPU starves an 8 GPU tray with eight NICs; two is the standard layout. NICs — rule of thumb: one NIC per GPU "rail optimized" for training, one per two GPUs for inference. The advisor shows whether you meet the training bandwidth tier customers expect this year. Memory — populate all channels, and keep host RAM around half of GPU HBM so checkpointing stays smooth. 5 year cost — capex and power per GPU and your break even hourly cost at full and partial utilization, against what the market pays this year. The rack bench A rack is a 42U elevation. Add compute trays in the middle, ToR switches at the top, power and storage at the bottom zones are hints; the Add button finds the best free spot . Every component has height in U and a power draw, and validation checks units used, weight, cost — and above all kilowatts against the rack's limit . Rack density is the real limit of the whole game. An 8 GPU H100 tray draws roughly 10 kW; four per rack is already 40 kW, the edge of air cooling. The rack's cooling interface air / RDHx / DLC / immersion must match what your hall can serve — see Power and cooling power and cooling.md . The validation panel also shows the tray's scale up domain how many GPUs NVLink joins into one memory domain , which matters for big model workloads. Design Lab img/design.png The tray bench: sockets, live validation and the sizing advisor. Liquid cooled racks img/campus dlc.png Dense liquid cooled racks in a DLC hall — note the coolant plumbing. From design to floor A saved design is only paper. The Warehouse shows, per design, how many racks are ready to deploy and exactly which parts are missing — with an order all missing button that buys everything, spares included. A rack can only be deployed when every part is in the warehouse and the hall has power, cooling headroom and a free slot. Then comes installation and commissioning burn in , which finds failed optics and GPUs before customers do. Skipping burn in ships dead GPUs. Spares Parts fail at a steady rate: GPUs, PSUs, NICs, NVMe drives, DIMMs, CPUs and switches all break. A spare on your shelf swaps in within a month; without one, the vendor RMA takes roughly four months — during which the rack misses SLAs and earns nothing while it still depreciates. Orders include the advised spares by default, and the Warehouse's spares table shows have vs advised per part with a one click top up. See Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md . Related: Networking and clusters networking and clusters.md for what happens after the rack is online, and Money and operations money and operations.md for selling racks at end of life.

title: Networking and clusters
text: Networking and clusters Scale up versus scale out, fabrics and oversubscription, and how the Supercomputer screen turns racks into one machine. A cluster is racks plus a network fabric. Racks that aren't clustered can still serve inference straight from the Customers screen, but a training customer rents one big coherent machine — that's what you build here. Two kinds of network Scale up NVLink links GPUs inside a node or rack at TB/s and makes them act like one GPU with one memory domain. Model parallel and MoE traffic lives here. Contracts state the scale up domain they need a 72 GPU NVLink domain comes from a GB200 NVL72 rack . Scale out InfiniBand / Ethernet links nodes and racks at 25–100+ GB/s per GPU. Data parallel gradients cross this one. Contracts also state the GB/s per GPU they expect. Wrong balance between the two means idle GPUs. Training needs both; inference mostly needs memory and tokens per second. The Supercomputer screen 1. Pick racks — any online racks not already in a cluster, across all halls. 2. Wire the network — the easy way is Auto design for TRAINING finds the cheapest fabric that meets the year's expected GB/s per GPU or Auto design for INFERENCE cheaper still . The advanced panel exposes everything: scale out tech InfiniBand NDR/XDR, Spectrum X, 400G/800G Ethernet, RoCE, Ultra Ethernet , topology fat tree rail optimized, fat tree, single domain, dragonfly, torus ish , leaf and spine switches, node→leaf and leaf→spine cables, and an oversubscription slider. 3. Read the stats — accelerators, scale up domain, FP8 compute, memory, power, effective GB/s per GPU, bisection bandwidth and network capex. 4. What can this machine do? — a per model table showing whether the training state fits tokens/s and MFU and whether weights fit for serving tokens/s, time to first token, tensor parallel size . 5. BUILD CLUSTER . Existing machines can be unclustered and re clustered at any time — dissolve one, adjust the rack selection, rebuild. Clusters show in the hall as colored markers, and each rack's inspector says which cluster and customer it belongs to. Supercomputer builder img/supercomputer.png Pick racks, wire the fabric, and see what the machine can train or serve. Oversubscription Spine uplinks can carry less than the sum of leaf downlinks — that ratio is oversubscription . 2:1 cuts your spine cost while slowing collective operations. Pick 1:1 for training big all reduce traffic punishes congestion and 2–4:1 for inference , where it is usually fine and much cheaper. The stats panel flags effective GB/s per GPU below the year's training tier. Design rules of thumb One NIC per GPU, rail optimized , for training trays; half that for inference the tray sizing advisor checks this . The scale up domain decides which models you can serve efficiently — MoE expert parallelism and huge model inference want everything inside one NVLink domain. At scale, the network IS the computer : past a few hundred GPUs, bisection bandwidth and failure rates dominate training efficiency. The 256 accelerator mission exists to teach this. HBM and the KV cache decide inference capacity: GPU memory holds the weights plus every active request's cache. No room to batch users means tokens/s you can't sell. The "what you need to buy" checks on contracts verify this for you. Fewer, bigger switches higher radix mean fewer tiers, fewer hops and less cabling power per GPU — a generation of 102.4 Tb/s switch silicon halves switch count for the same fabric. Internet transit Customer facing bandwidth lives on the Build screen: buy IP transit circuits, watch demand Gb/s against your uplink capacity, and — before signing SLA heavy contracts — buy a second carrier on a physically diverse path . One circuit is one backhoe away from an outage see Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md . Related: Customers and contracts customers and contracts.md for assigning clusters, Hardware roadmap hardware roadmap.md for how fabrics evolve.

title: Customers and contracts
text: Customers and contracts Training versus inference offers, fit verdicts, the Easy Path, SLAs, renewals and the ramp window — how capacity becomes revenue. Customers pay for capacity in two ways, and the hardware they need differs: Training customers rent a big coherent cluster by the GPU hour. Offers state a minimum accelerator count, a price per GPU hour, and network requirements — a scale up domain size e.g. 72 and GB/s per GPU. Training is compute and network bound. Inference customers pay per million tokens. Offers state a target tokens/s and a price per Mtok. Inference is memory bandwidth bound: GPUs with more HBM capacity and bandwidth hold bigger models and bigger KV caches, serving more users per replica. Each offer also shows its archetype startup, lab, enterprise, sovereign , the model, the duration in months, an SLA availability target, and a deadline by which you must sign or the offer disappears. Customers and contracts img/customers.png Market offers with live fit verdicts and what you still lack. Offers lead with what they pay: monthly revenue, total value img/contract offers.png Offers lead with what they pay: monthly revenue, total value and profit after power. The requirements fold open when you want the detail. Fit verdicts Every offer carries a live verdict computed against your actual fleet: ✓ CAN SERVE NOW — an existing cluster meets every check. Sign and go live immediately. ◔ CAN BUILD IN TIME — you can buy and commission hardware before the ramp window closes. ✗ NEED MORE / DIFFERENT HARDWARE — below, the What you need to buy box names the exact racks template, quantity, tier that would cover the contract, when they would be ready, and whether that fits the ramp window — plus any hall gaps power, cooling, floor you'd need to close first. If nothing on the market can meet it, it says so: wait for a later GPU generation. ✗ NO CLUSTER YET — build one on the Supercomputer screen. Checks compare need vs have: accelerators, memory, scale up domain, scale out bandwidth, and so on. If the verdict isn't "ready", the screen also shows your pipeline — accelerators free online, commissioning, in warehouse, on order. The Easy Path EASY PATH — do it all for me signs the contract, orders the racks, installs plant, deploys, builds the fabric and assigns the contract as parts arrive. Watch progress as Easy path projects on the Overview screen Order & build → Burn in → Cluster → Assign → LIVE . It's a learning tool and a convenience; doing the steps yourself from the same "what you need to buy" list works identically. Just order the racks is the middle option — you buy, then handle deployment, clustering and assignment yourself. Signing, ramp window and SLAs You can sign an offer you can't serve yet: after signing you get a ramp window about four months by default to deploy. No revenue and no SLA clock runs until you go live — miss the window and the customer walks, with a reputation hit. Deploy by building or picking a cluster, or use serve straight from racks for inference without a clustering step. While serving, the panel shows months served and SLA misses . Misses come from outages, failures and overloaded uplinks see Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md ; too many and the contract sours. You can update which clusters serve a contract as your fleet changes, or release it back to pending. Renewals Delivered contracts compound: satisfied customers come back with renewal offers — bigger, at a premium over the original — and they sort to the top of the market list. Renewals are cheaper than acquisitions; a contract book balanced across training and inference rides out demand cycles instead of chasing them. Reputation The ★ reputation in the top bar drives the quality of offers you receive. It rises with delivered contracts and uptime, and falls with SLA misses, missed ramp windows, outages, fires and customer defaults. Related: Networking and clusters networking and clusters.md for building what the checks demand, Money and operations money and operations.md for the P&L behind a signed deal.

title: Money and operations
text: Money and operations Cash, loans and interest, depreciation, staffing, hardware lifecycle and resale — everything on the Operations screen. The core equation, visible on the Overview plaques: revenue − burn = net , where burn is power + staff + support + interest, and the net figure is stated after depreciation. Utilization is everything — an idle rack earns nothing while it still draws power and depreciates. Net worth = cash − debt + assets at residual value : only profitable months compound, borrowed scale does not. Cash, loans and bankruptcy Loans land in cash instantly and interest accrues monthly; the credit limit grows with your installed assets. Repay in chunks or all at once when cash allows — interest is a silent burn line, so gear up for builds, not for idle balances. Three consecutive months of negative cash is bankruptcy and the campaign ends with your creditors closing you down. The Next month preview on the Overview screen shows cash after next month and your runway at the current burn — check it before every big order. Learner mode cannot go bankrupt. Team Racks don't run themselves. The staffing rule: one ops technician per 10 online racks , plus a liquid cooling specialist once a DLC/immersion hall has online racks, plus a network engineer per 1,024 clustered accelerators — a skeleton crew of one even when empty. Understaffing multiplies failure rates and slows repairs; the screen shows the exact effect. Hire ahead of the fleet, not after it: a failed rack costs far more than an early hire. Operating policy Two dials with real trade offs: Burn in — how long racks soak before going live. Skipping it ships dead GPUs; longer soak catches more failures at the price of extra months of lead time. Maintenance — reactive no fee , preventive, or premium. Higher tiers cut failure rates for a monthly per rack fee. Hardware lifecycle and resale The lifecycle table lists every rack with its age, its accelerator, its residual value percentage and a sale price — sorted worst first, with advice per rack. GPUs lose value to successor generations faster than to wear: under the yearly cadence, resale timing is part of the business model. Sell while residual value is real; a rack must be unclustered first, and quick sale pays less than residual value as the convenience discount. The Learning path has a mission for your first decommissioned rack, because a fleet that never refreshes ends up running hardware no customer wants. Clearing stock Leftover parts in the warehouse can be sold from Clear warehouse stock at a discount to list. Useful after design changes and cancelled builds; don't let a stale inventory become a junk drawer. Vendor relationships and frameworks Buying from a vendor builds a relationship : better allocation multipliers on constrained parts and relationship pricing. Frameworks go further — commit to a spend over a set term for a discount on that vendor's parts, with a deposit paid up front. A framework that expires with its commitment unmet costs a penalty on the shortfall. Frameworks matter most when a hot generation is allocation constrained see Hardware roadmap hardware roadmap.md . Market competition The Operations screen tracks rival operators: their share, their fleet size, and whether they price above or below list. When rivals undercut, incoming offers are priced down; when your scale commands the market, offers are priced up. The price index tells you which world you're in. Related: Customers and contracts customers and contracts.md for the revenue side, Energy and the spot market energy and spot.md for one of the largest burn lines.

title: Energy and the spot market
text: Energy and the spot market PPAs and take or pay power, the spot utility rate, and selling idle GPU capacity hour by hour. Power is one of your largest operating costs, and your PUE power and cooling.md sets how much of it goes to overhead. The Energy screen Facility drawer → Energy tab manages both sides: what you pay for electricity and what idle hardware earns while it waits for a contract. The power position The top panel shows your facility draw in MW against your committed contracts. With no contracts, you buy 100% at the spot utility rate , which mean reverts toward a baseline but spikes during energy crisis events — sometimes painfully. The projected monthly bill and blended rate tell you what your halls actually cost to run. PPAs — take or pay power A power purchase agreement is a long contract to buy fixed MW from a plant at a fixed price, paid whether you use the power or not. Plant offers arrive most months from grid, solar, gas, hydro and nuclear sources, and each card shows: Price vs the current spot rate Firmness — the share of months the plant actually delivers a supplier failure means curtailment or fallback to spot Oversubscription limit — you may draw above your commit up to a limit, billed at an overage multiple; beyond that, you're back on spot Take or pay — the fixed monthly bill for the committed MW; unused surplus is resold at a discount PPAs are cheaper than spot and hedge price spikes, but they punish over commitment: signing a big block before your load exists means paying for unused megawatts. Size contracts to your steady, predictable draw and let spot cover the peaks. The screen does the arithmetic for you — each offer shows how much cheaper or dearer than spot it would be at today's load, and it warns you outright when nothing is drawing yet. The spot GPU market The flip side: a floating spot price per GPU hour , driven by market demand the fill rate . When demand spikes, idle clusters earn well; when it crashes, they barely cover power. You can: Offer individual racks — no cluster needed; tick them on the Energy screen or from the rack inspector in the hall. They earn while waiting for a contract. Offer whole clusters — a cluster serving no contract can earn on spot. Set a reserve price — you never sell below your floor. A rack on spot leaves the market automatically once a contract takes it. Spot is pre emptible : committed contracts always win, so treat spot as a bridge, not a business model. The Codex's spot vs reserved concept nags you when online racks are idle and not on spot — idle GPUs still cost power and depreciation. How they fit together A balanced position looks like: a PPA or two covering your contracted baseline load, spot power absorbing the peaks, and every idle rack offered on the spot market until a customer signs. When an energy crisis hits the utility rate, the PPA block is the part of your bill that doesn't move — that's the hedge working. When a viral model launch floods inference demand, spot is where idle memory rich GPUs pay off. Related: Customers and contracts customers and contracts.md for the reserved side, Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md for crisis events, Strategy tips strategy tips.md .

title: Hardware roadmap
text: Hardware roadmap Keynotes, pre orders, lead times and allocation — knowing what ships next decides when you buy, build and sell. Silicon is announced at keynotes months before it ships. The game fires keynotes on their real calendar dates — GTC spring , Computex May/June , SC November , OCP, and AMD's Advancing AI events — and each one pauses the clock with a keynote card explaining the technology, what it changes in your hall, and the one thing to remember. The Roadmap tab in Procurement lists every past keynote with a Read the keynote button and shows the next one coming. Pre orders and allocation After a keynote, announced parts become pre orderable : Pre orders open at the keynote, never earlier than 12 months before the ship date You pay a launch premium and queue behind the hyperscalers ; delivery lands after the ship date Cancelling refunds most of what you paid — a pre order is a cheap option on supply Even regular orders of hot parts carry per quarter allocation caps ; vendor relationships and frameworks raise your allocation see Money and operations money and operations.md If you wait instead, you pay the going rate and stand in the queue with everyone else — hot generations sell out before they ship. The shape of the campaign A few beats worth planning around dates as they land in game : GTC 2021 — Grace. A roadmap keynote: an Arm CPU built to sit next to GPUs over NVLink C2C. Nothing to buy for years; note the direction. GTC 2022 — Hopper H100. FP8 Transformer Engine, NVLink 4 at 900 GB/s between GPUs, ~3.35 TB/s HBM3, 700 W per SXM GPU — an 8 GPU node is ~10 kW. A GPU generation is a power and cooling project first and a chip purchase second. 2023 — GH200, Spectrum X, MI300X, H200. Memory becomes the story: MI300X brings 192 GB of HBM3, and H200 shows that when a workload is memory bound, faster memory is worth more than faster math. Ethernet becomes a real alternative to InfiniBand for scale out. GTC 2024 — Blackwell. GB200 NVL72 links 72 GPUs into one liquid cooled ~120 kW rack NVLink 5 at 1.8 TB/s per GPU . Air cooled halls cannot host it at all; the floor needs a CDU loop. Computex 2024 — the yearly cadence. All vendors move to annual generations. Everything you buy depreciates faster; resale timing becomes part of the business model. GTC 2025 — Blackwell Ultra, Vera Rubin roadmap. GB300 drops into GB200 class racks: same ~120 kW, so the hall you built keeps working. Rubin racks will draw considerably more — plan bigger feeds and CDUs early. Oct 2025 — Vera Rubin orders open. Longer queues than any prior generation; earlier generation prices soften as buyers wait. Sell older racks while residual value holds. GTC 2026 — Rubin Ultra, 102.4 Tb/s switches. 576 GPU NVLink domains; bigger switch silicon means fewer tiers and hops per GPU. When to buy Plan the building two generations ahead. Racks change yearly; power and cooling plants last decades. Buy transformers and CDU capacity for the rack that ships next, not the one shipping today. Pre order at the keynote when the part changes your market — e.g. a rack format that unlocks contracts you can't serve — and treat the cancellation loss as the price of a place in the queue. Sell into strength. When a generation lands, its predecessor becomes a discounted workhorse: reassign it to inference or spot, or sell it while residual value is real. Watch the calendar beats. The 2023 demand shock slashes allocation and slips in transit GPU orders; later, vendors reward operators with demonstrated deployments — a campus that ships on schedule gets first call on the next generation. The Codex's accelerator timeline view shows every generation with memory, bandwidth, power and scale up — the fastest way to compare what to buy. Related: Hardware lifecycle money and operations.md · Servers and racks servers and racks.md · Power and cooling power and cooling.md .

title: Incidents and resilience
text: Incidents and resilience Fires, chiller trips, outages, supply shocks and customer defaults — what can go wrong and how to be the operator it doesn't happen to. After an opening grace period, roughly one world event fires every few months. Each one tests a decision you made earlier — or teaches you the decision you should have made. The event log on the Overview screen explains the lesson every time. Now and then a decision with two honest answers. Ignore it a img/story decision.png Now and then a decision with two honest answers. Ignore it and the offer lapses after three months. The incident catalog Utility outage. A weak power chain no UPS, no battery string, an undersized generator, no transfer switch means running jobs restart from checkpoint, every serving contract takes an SLA miss, and reputation drops. A complete chain — UPS + battery + generator + transfer switch, sized N+1 — rides through with zero customer impact. The Outage protection panel on the Build screen shows your tier and the exact gap to close. Fiber cut. A backhoe takes out a fiber route. With a second carrier on a physically diverse path , customers never notice; with one circuit, it's an outage and a reputation hit. Two carriers is a Learning path mission for a reason. Fire. One online rack burns. A hall whose power chain is at N tier or better contains the fire to a short rebuild; in any weaker hall the rack is destroyed, the rebuild takes many months and reputation suffers. Chiller trip. A compressor fault drops the cooling loop for hours: every serving contract takes an SLA miss and emergency pumping costs money per affected rack. N+1 chillers with automatic switchover keep the water cold while one unit is repaired. Energy crisis. The spot utility rate jumps. PPAs cover the committed block see Energy and the spot market energy and spot.md ; a lower PUE shrinks the exposed part. Heatwave. Dry coolers derate in hot ambient air and extra chiller energy costs money. Warm water liquid cooling tolerates hot days far better than air cooled halls. Customer default. A serving customer goes bankrupt mid deal: the contract dies, a month of expected revenue never lands, reputation drops, and the cluster suddenly idles. A balanced contract book across several customers absorbs it. Supply chain shock. A fab substrate shortage and a port strike: every in transit order slips. Dual sourcing and safety stock are insurance, not waste. Demand shock March 2023 . ChatGPT goes viral: allocation is slashed and accelerators already in your pipeline slip. Lead times quoted in a soft market are fiction in a hot one. Hardware failures always Independent of events, parts fail at a steady rate — GPUs, PSUs, NICs, NVMe drives, DIMMs, CPUs, ToR switches. A spare on the shelf puts the rack back in about a month; the vendor RMA without a spare takes roughly four, during which the rack misses SLAs and earns nothing while still depreciating. The Warehouse spares table tracks have vs advised per part; orders bundle the advised spares by default. Understaffing multiplies failure rates and slows repairs see Money and operations money and operations.md . The preparation checklist 1. Complete power chain per hall, N+1 before signing high SLA contracts 2. Two carriers on diverse paths 3. N+1 chillers once a central plant exists 4. Spares shelf at the advised level, checked monthly 5. Staffing at or ahead of need 6. A PPA block covering baseline load 7. A contract book spread across customers and workload kinds Thermal view of a campus img/campus thermal.png Press T in the hall: seeing heat early is half of preventing failures. Resilience is not a cost center — it's what tier III customers pay for, and what keeps one bad month from ending the campaign.

title: Strategy tips
text: Strategy tips Habits that separate a thriving AI factory from a beautiful hall full of idle GPUs. Deliberately qualitative — balance numbers shift with tuning, the habits don't. The end screen: how the story finished, your revenue and cas img/end screen.png The end screen: how the story finished, your revenue and cash over eight years, your best deal, your worst incident and how you stacked up against the rivals. Buy before you need Lead times and allocation punish just in time thinking. Order transformers, plant and racks for the contracts you expect , not just the ones you've signed. When a keynote announces a part that changes your market, a pre order is a cheap place in the queue — you can cancel most of it back if plans change. Grow the boring parts first Power and cooling cap everything. Expand the feed and the cooling plant ahead of the racks that will use them, and keep both gauges out of the red zone before you deploy. A second hall takes longer than you think — start it before you need it, and use it to separate air cooled and liquid cooled fleets. Match hardware to workload Memory capacity and bandwidth decide inference economics; compute, scale up domains and fabric decide training economics. Read the contract checks before buying anything, let the "what you need to buy" box do the arithmetic, and don't buy premium fabric for inference or starved memory for serving. Utilization is the business Idle GPUs still burn power and depreciation. Put every idle online rack on the spot market, chase the ramp window on signed contracts, and prefer renewals over hunting for fresh customers — delivered contracts compound reputation and bring follow on offers. Run it like an operator Keep the spares shelf at the advised level; the RMA months you skip are the outages you avoid Hire ahead of the fleet; understaffed sites fail more and repair slower Choose burn in and maintenance policies deliberately — shipping dead GPUs and skipping prevention both cost more than they save Two carriers on diverse paths, N+1 power before high SLA contracts Mind the money Watch the Next month preview before committing cash: deliveries, burn ins, completions, expiring offers, warnings. Watch runway and never let cash go negative for long — bankruptcy is a short walk from one over ordered quarter. Borrow to build earning capacity, not to cover burn; interest accrues monthly whether the GPUs work or not. Sell hardware on a cadence Under the yearly cadence, GPUs lose value to successor generations faster than to wear. Refresh on rhythm, reassign the previous generation to inference or spot, and sell racks while residual value is real. A fleet that never refreshes ends up running hardware no customer wants to pay for. Hedge what you can't control A PPA sized to your steady load turns energy crises into non events; over committing turns them into monthly losses. Blend contract kinds training and inference and customers so a default or a demand dip doesn't idle the campus. Learn the stack The Codex's "Datacenter 101" verdicts tell you whether you need each concept right now — read them, click Show me where , and close gaps in order. Missions pay you to learn the whole stack; finish the Learning path before you decide which habits to skip. Down the cold aisle img/campus aisle.png Cold aisle discipline: containment, labels and no surprises. Keep it boring The endgame scoring rewards net worth, reliability and scale — and all three come from the same place: racks bought, filled, refreshed and sold on schedule, with no fires, no outages and no missed ramp windows. Spectacular is what it looks like when you didn't prepare. Related: Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md · Money and operations money and operations.md · Hardware roadmap hardware roadmap.md .

title: FAQ
text: FAQ Fifteen questions every operator asks sooner or later. 1. Which mode should I pick? Pick Learner if a chiller is a mystery — it adds explainers everywhere, and you can't go bankrupt. Operator is the intended experience with the guided planner and checklists. Tycoon strips the help. You can cycle modes any time from the top bar. The Easy Path "do it for me" is available in every mode. 2. Do I need to know hardware to play? No. The tutorial walks you from first customer to first revenue, the Learning path pays you to learn each system, and the in game Codex explains every concept and part with a live "do I need this right now?" verdict. Start with Your first hour first hour.md . 3. How do I actually make money? Sign contracts, deploy hardware that meets their checks in time, and keep utilization high. Revenue minus power, staff, support, depreciation and interest is profit. Idle GPUs on the spot market cover part of their own cost while they wait. 4. Why does my order take months to arrive? Everything has a lead time, hot GPUs have per quarter allocation caps, and shocks can slip in transit orders further. Order ahead of need; missions teach this first for a reason. See Hardware roadmap hardware roadmap.md . 5. Why can't I place my rack? A deploy needs every part of the design in the warehouse, plus hall power, cooling headroom and a free slot. The Warehouse and Build screens list exactly what's missing — use order all missing . 6. What is commissioning / burn in? The soak period after installation: power on, firmware, burn in tests. It catches dead GPUs and optics before customers do. Its length is a policy you set in Operations — skipping it ships dead silicon. 7. Air or liquid cooling? Air works to roughly 20–25 kW per rack, rear door heat exchangers stretch toward 40 kW, and direct to chip liquid with CDUs is required beyond that — GB200 NVL72 class racks ~120 kW are liquid only. See Power and cooling power and cooling.md . 8. What is PUE and why should I care? Total facility power ÷ IT power. You pay the overhead every month, so efficient cooling directly cuts your power bill — especially with PPAs energy and spot.md pricing every MWh. 9. Training or inference contracts? Whatever your hardware fits. Training pays by the GPU hour and demands scale up domains and fabric bandwidth; inference pays per token and rewards memory capacity and bandwidth. A balanced book of both rides out demand cycles. 10. What oversubscription should I pick? 1:1 for training clusters congestion slows collectives , 2–4:1 for inference much cheaper, rarely missed . The Supercomputer screen's auto design buttons pick sensibly for you. See Networking and clusters networking and clusters.md . 11. Should I sign a PPA? Usually yes, sized to your steady load: it hedges energy crisis spikes. But take or pay means you buy the committed MW even when idle, so don't over commit before the load exists. See Energy and the spot market energy and spot.md . 12. My contract says "awaiting deployment" — what now? You signed; the ramp window about four months is ticking. Build/buy the hardware, cluster it on the Supercomputer screen, then assign the cluster — or serve straight from racks for inference. Miss the window and the customer walks with a reputation hit. See Customers and contracts customers and contracts.md . 13. A rack failed — why, and how do I fix it fast? Parts fail at a steady rate. A spare on the shelf swaps in within about a month; without one, the vendor RMA takes roughly four. Check the spares table on the Warehouse and keep it at the advised level. See Incidents and resilience incidents and resilience.md . 14. When should I sell old racks? When residual value is still real — typically as the successor generation lands and demand shifts to it. The Operations lifecycle table sorts worst first and advises per rack. Sell while the hardware is still a discounted workhorse, not a paperweight. 15. How does the campaign end? December 2028 brings a scored report: rating, net worth, lifetime revenue, peak accelerators, contracts completed, reputation. Alternatively, three consecutive months of negative cash ends everything early in bankruptcy Learner mode excepted . See Money and operations money and operations.md . Still stuck? The Glossary glossary.md defines the words, and the in game Codex explains every part.

title: Glossary
text: Glossary Forty one datacenter terms, one line each, alphabetical. The Codex img/codex.png The in game Codex: every part and concept, with tradeoffs. Allocation — per quarter caps on how many units of a constrained part usually GPUs you may buy; vendor relationships and frameworks raise yours. ATS automatic transfer switch — gear that moves hall load from the utility to your generators without human action; part of the N+1 chain. Bisection bandwidth — the total traffic rate a fabric can carry across its middle; the headline number for whether a cluster trains well. Burn in — the soak test after rack installation power on, firmware, stress tests that finds dead GPUs and optics before customers do. CDU coolant distribution unit — the pump and isolation box between a liquid cooling plant and the cold plates on chips in DLC halls. Chiller — central plant that makes cold water for CRAHs and CDUs; paired with a tower or dry cooler that rejects heat to outside air. Cluster — online racks plus a network fabric wired into one machine that contracts are assigned to. Commissioning — the full bring up of a rack installation plus burn in ; its length is a policy choice in Operations. CRAH computer room air handler — the fans and coil unit of air cooled halls; pushes cold air through the floor and pulls hot air back. DLC direct to chip liquid cooling — coolant through cold plates on GPUs/CPUs; required beyond roughly 40 kW per rack. Easy Path — the button that signs a contract and orders, installs, deploys, clusters and assigns the hardware for you. Fabric — the leaf/spine network switches and cables that turns a group of racks into one cluster. Fat tree — the classic multi tier cluster topology; rail optimized variants give each GPU its own leaf path. Genset — diesel or gas generator set that carries the hall through long utility outages. HBM high bandwidth memory — stacked memory on accelerators; its capacity and bandwidth decide how big a model fits and how fast it serves. Heat rejection — cooling capacity in kW; must meet or exceed IT load or hardware fails roughly three times more often. Inference — serving a trained model to users; memory bandwidth bound, priced per million tokens. KV cache — per request state that inference keeps in GPU memory alongside the weights; its size caps how many users you can batch. Lead time — months between ordering a part and holding it; the reason to order ahead of need. MFU model FLOPS utilization — the share of peak compute a training run actually achieves; low MFU usually blames the network. NIC network interface card — the host's scale out port; rule of thumb is one per GPU for training, one per two for inference. NVLink — NVIDIA's scale up interconnect with NVSwitch , joining GPUs inside a rack into one memory domain at TB/s. N+1 redundancy — one more unit generator, battery string, chiller than strictly needed, so any single failure has zero customer impact. Oversubscription — the ratio of leaf downlink capacity to spine uplink capacity; 1:1 for training, 2–4:1 for inference. PPA power purchase agreement — a long contract for fixed MW at a fixed price from a plant, paid whether or not you draw it. PUE power usage effectiveness — total facility power ÷ IT power; 1.0 is perfect, 1.1–1.5 typical, and you pay the difference monthly. Rack density — kW per rack; the real physical limit of a hall air ≈ 20–25 kW, RDHx toward 40, DLC beyond . Ramp window — the months after signing a contract to get serving default about four ; miss it and the customer walks. RDHx rear door heat exchanger — a water coil on the rack's back door that cools exhaust air without plumbing the servers. Residual value — what a rack is still worth as it ages and generations pass; quick sale pays a fraction of it. RMA return merchandise authorization — the months long vendor repair path for a failed part when you have no spare on the shelf. Scale out — InfiniBand/Ethernet networking between nodes at 25–100+ GB/s per GPU; carries data parallel traffic. Scale up — NVLink class linking of GPUs inside a node or rack into one domain; carries model parallel and MoE traffic. SLA service level agreement — the availability a contract demands commonly 95–99.5% ; misses cost reputation and renewals. Spot market GPU — selling idle GPUs hour by hour at a floating price with no commitment; pre emptible by any contract. Spot market power — buying electricity at the volatile utility rate instead of under a PPA. Take or pay — the PPA clause: you pay for the committed megawatts whether you use them or not; surplus is resold at a discount. Training — renting a coherent cluster to train a model; compute and network bound, priced per GPU hour. Transformer / switchgear — the hall's power feed; steps utility voltage down and caps maximum IT load in kW. TTFT time to first token — how long an inference request waits before its first token; the latency number customers feel. UPS uninterruptible power supply — inverter plus battery or flywheel that rides through grid dips while generators start. Related: the in game Codex carries the full encyclopedia with per part engineering notes.
